content: The Care for Child Development Participant Manual is a comprehensive guide developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) to improve the care and development of young children. 1. Introduction to Child Care and Development Children require attentive care to ensure their survival and healthy development. This includes recognizing when they are hungry or unwell, meeting their physical needs, protecting them from harm, and providing love, attention, and opportunities to learn. From birth, children form bonds with specific adults, learning essential skills through these relationships, which prepare them for life. This manual supports families and caregivers in raising healthy, happy children, even in challenging circumstances such as poverty or other adversities. 2. Course Objectives By the end of the course, participants will be able to: Observe and identify interactions between a child and their primary caregiver. Counsel families on activities that strengthen the bond between the child and caregiver. Advise families on age-appropriate play and communication activities to stimulate the child’s growth and development. Participants will focus on observing caregivers with their children and using effective communication skills to provide counseling. 3. Course Methods and Materials The course involves reading, observing, and practicing counseling techniques with families and caregivers. Materials provided include: A participant manual, which you are currently reading. Counseling cards, which suggest activities to enhance a child’s development. These cards serve as a reference for advising caregivers on play and communication activities as the child grows. A checklist to guide the assessment of a child’s care and help families solve problems while learning how to play and communicate with their child. Additional materials such as videos and role-playing exercises to practice skills in real-life settings. 4. Role of the Caregiver The caregiver is the most important person in a young child’s life. They are responsible for feeding, protecting, and nurturing the child, as well as responding to the child’s needs. In most cases, the caregiver is the child’s mother, but it could also be the father, a relative, or another family member. In some communities, caregiving responsibilities are shared among multiple individuals, such as grandparents, aunts, or older siblings. Building strong relationships with caregivers is essential to improving the lives of children in the community. 5. Recommendations for Care Based on Age Newborns (Birth to 1 Week): Encourage skin-to-skin contact, gentle soothing, and breastfeeding. If the mother does not breastfeed, advise her to hold the child close, make eye contact, and talk or sing to the child during feeding. Infants (1 Week to 6 Months): Promote activities that allow the baby to see, hear, and move freely. Encourage caregivers to talk to the baby, make eye contact, and respond to the baby’s sounds and smiles. Children (6 Months to 2 Years): Suggest interactive play, such as hiding toys for the child to find or stacking objects. Encourage caregivers to name objects, ask simple questions, and respond to the child’s attempts to communicate. Children (2 Years and Older): Recommend activities that involve counting, sorting, and storytelling. Encourage caregivers to teach songs, play games, and talk about pictures or books with the child. 6. Addressing Challenges in Caregiving If caregivers feel too stressed or burdened to play and communicate with the child, listen to their concerns and help them identify someone who can support them. Build their confidence by demonstrating simple activities they can do with the child. If caregivers lack toys, suggest using clean, safe household objects or making simple toys. If the child is not responding or seems slow to learn, encourage extra play and communication activities, check the child’s hearing and vision, and refer the family to specialized services if needed. If the child is being treated harshly, recommend positive discipline strategies, such as praising good behavior, understanding the child’s emotions, and offering choices instead of saying “don’t.” 7. Counseling Techniques Look, Ask, and Listen: Observe how caregivers interact with their children and how they engage in play and communication. Praise: Reinforce caregivers’ efforts and build their confidence by acknowledging their positive actions. Advise: Provide suggestions for improving caregiving practices, if necessary. Solve Problems: Identify and address any difficulties caregivers may face in providing care. Check Understanding: Ensure caregivers understand and remember the advice given, so they can implement it effectively at home. 8. Special Considerations for Health Workers Health workers trained in Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) may counsel caregivers on child development, particularly for children who are underweight or anemic. However, their time may be limited to working with sick children in acute-care settings. Other counselors can use these guidelines with families of all children, whether sick or well, in various community settings. 9. Building Relationships with Caregivers Greet caregivers warmly and build positive relationships with them. This approach fosters trust and enables you to make a meaningful impact on the lives of children in your community. 10. Key Messages for Caregivers Show affection and love to your child. Be attentive to your child’s interests and respond to them. Praise your child for trying to learn new skills. Engage in play and communication activities that are appropriate for your child’s age and developmental stage. This manual emphasizes the importance of nurturing care, effective communication, and interactive play in promoting a child’s healthy development. It provides practical tools and strategies for caregivers and health workers to support children’s growth and well-being.
